question: The Akbar Nama, written by Abul Fazal, has the Ain-i-Akbari as its:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Third volume.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Akbar Nama is a three-part work by Abul Fazal, and its third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari (अकबरनामा का तीसरा खंड — आइन-ए-अकबरी)

 

• Volume 1 deals with Akbar's ancestors, and volume 2 narrates the events of Akbar's reign.

 

• Volume 3, the Ain-i-Akbari, covers Akbar's administration, army, revenue and the geography of his empire.

 

• Abul Fazal was Akbar's chief advisor and the son of Shaikh Mubarak Nagori; he authored in Persian.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Abul Fazal's brother Faizi was the poet laureate of Akbar.

 

• The Ain-i-Akbari is a valuable source for Mughal revenue and mansabdari statistics.

 

• Shah Jahan's biography Shahjahan Nama was by Inayat Khan.

 

• Aurangzeb's Alamgir Nama was written by Muhammad Kazim.

 

• The Ain-i-Akbari contains tables of the mansabdars, revenue rates and provinces, so historians rely on it as the main source on the Mughal administration of Akbar's period.

 

NOTE

 

• First volume (Option 1): The first volume is about the ancestors of Akbar from Timur through Babur and Humayun, not the administrative survey that forms the Ain-i-Akbari.

 

• Second volume (Option 2): The second volume records the events of Akbar's reign in chronological order, and it is different from the survey of administration known as Ain-i-Akbari.

 

• Introductory chapter only (Option 3): Calling it only an introductory chapter is wrong because the Ain-i-Akbari is a full independent volume of substantial length dealing with administration and geography.

question: The Persian translation of the Mahabharata prepared at Akbar's Maktab Khana was known as:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Razmnama.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Persian version of the Mahabharata was called Razmnama (Book of Wars), translated by Abul Fazal and Abdul Qadir Badauni among others (रज़्मनामा — महाभारत का फारसी अनुवाद)

 

• In 1574 Akbar founded the Maktab Khana, the House of Translation, at Fatehpur Sikri.

 

• The translation bureau rendered Sanskrit and other works into Persian, which was the official language.

 

• It helped a cultural exchange that matched Akbar's religious toleration.

 

• Translation work in the Maktab Khana helped Persian speaking nobles understand Hindu texts, and it formed part of the effort to build a common cultural outlook across communities.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rahim translated Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati into Persian.

 

• Badauni authored the Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, critical of Akbar.

 

• Akbar's reign is called the golden period of literature.

 

• The Ibadat Khana was built at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575.

 

• Other Sanskrit works rendered into Persian under Akbar include the Ramayana, the Atharvaveda and the Lilavati, together with the Singhasan Battisi.

 

NOTE

 

• Lilavati (Option 1): Lilavati is the mathematics treatise of Bhaskaracharya that was translated into Persian, and is a separate text and not the name of the Mahabharata's translation.

 

• Rajatarangini (Option 2): Rajatarangini is Kalhana's chronicle of Kashmir kings, translated into Persian in Akbar's time, but it is unrelated to the Mahabharata.

 

• Shahnama (Option 4): Shahnama is the Persian national epic of Firdausi, a work in Persian from Iran about Persian kings, and not the name of any Mahabharata translation.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Mansabdari system:

1. A mansab indicated both the rank and the salary of a noble.

2. Every officer of the Mughal state was given a mansab.

3. Mansabdars were required to live personally in the jagir whose revenue they drew.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: a mansab denoted the rank (zat) and the salary of a noble (मनसबदारी — पद एवं वेतन का सूचक)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: it was a ranking system in which every officer was given a mansab.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: mansabdars were not required to reside in the jagir they drew revenue from; they served at the emperor's pleasure and were transferred.

 

• The system organised both the military and the nobility.

 

• Because rank and pay were linked, a promotion in mansab brought more salary, and the emperor could appoint, promote or dismiss officers without any hereditary claim to the post.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The highest rank for nobles was usually 5000 zat, with princes receiving higher.

 

• Zat denotes personal rank and salary.

 

• Sawar rank indicated the number of cavalrymen maintained.

 

• The Mir Bakhshi paid the mansabdars and managed military appointments.

 

• Mansabdars were paid either in cash or through a jagir assignment, and the emperor could transfer the jagir to prevent a local power base from growing.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Statement 1 alone is incomplete because the claim that every officer received a mansab is also true; the system covered all officers of the state.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): The residence condition is untrue, which rules out any option carrying the third claim; mansabdars were transferred often and did not have to live on the jagir assigned to them.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three would include the false residence condition; the Mughal system deliberately kept nobles away from their jagirs to prevent local roots and rebellion.

question: Under Akbar's land revenue system, the method in which revenue was collected on the basis of a rough estimate, meaning payment based on the past, was called:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nasaq.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nasaq was the collection of land revenue on the basis of a rough estimate, i.e. payment based on past practice (नसक — अनुमान पर आधारित राजस्व)

 

• Batai (Galla Bakshi) was crop-sharing, and Zabti was assessment on the basis of land measurement.

 

• The Zabti system rested on measurement by Gaz, crop yields, prices and area cultivated, and was developed with Raja Todar Mal.

 

• These were three types of land revenue practised in Akbar's time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Todar Mal's arrangements are called the Todarmal Bandobast.

 

• The Zabt or Dahsala system fixed revenue on average yields of ten years.

 

• Sher Shah had earlier used land measurement with the Gaz-i-Sikandari.

 

• Kagaj-i-kham was a land revenue record.

 

• Under Akbar the rate was fixed at about one third of the produce under Zabti, which was applied in the north Indian provinces such as Delhi, Lahore and Agra.

 

NOTE

 

• Batai (Option 1): Batai, also called Galla Bakshi, shared the actual crop between peasant and state at harvest, so it relied on division and not on estimation from the past.

 

• Zabti (Option 2): Zabti collected revenue after measuring the land, using crop yields, prices and area cultivated, which is the opposite of a rough estimate.

 

• Kharaj (Option 4): Kharaj is the general Islamic term for land tax and was not the specific Akbar-era name for a rough-estimate assessment, which the chapter calls Nasaq.

question: Which Englishman became the first to visit Akbar's court, in 1585?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ralph Fitch.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ralph Fitch was the first Englishman to visit Akbar's court, in 1585 (राल्फ फिच — अकबर के दरबार में आने वाला पहला अंग्रेज)

 

• He travelled overland from England and recorded the commerce and society of Mughal India.

 

• Later English visitors came under Jahangir: Captain William Hawkins in 1608 and Sir Thomas Roe in 1615.

 

• Akbar's reign saw the Jesuit missions as well, such as Father Monserrat.

 

• Fitch's journey was a private commercial and exploratory trip, and his account was later useful to English merchants who formed the East India Company in 1600.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hawkins was called English Khan by Jahangir.

 

• Roe represented King James I.

 

• The East India Company was formed in 1600.

 

• Akbar's capital was moved to Lahore later in his reign.

 

• Ralph Fitch also visited Fatehpur Sikri and later travelled to Bengal, Burma and Malacca before returning to England.

 

• Fitch's report on Fatehpur Sikri described it as a city as large as London, a remark often quoted by historians.

 

NOTE

 

• William Hawkins (Option 1): William Hawkins arrived in 1608, in Jahangir's reign, as the East India Company's representative, so he was not the first Englishman at Akbar's court.

 

• Thomas Roe (Option 3): Thomas Roe reached Jahangir's court in 1615 as an ambassador of King James I and came after Akbar's death in 1605.

 

• Edward Terry (Option 4): Edward Terry accompanied Roe's embassy as a chaplain during Jahangir's reign, so he was not the Englishman who visited Akbar in 1585.

question: Akbar's tomb at Sikandra near Agra was:
option_2: Built by Nur Jahan in white marble
option_3: Started by Akbar and completed by Jahangir
solution_text:
The correct answer is Started by Akbar and completed by Jahangir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The tomb of Akbar at Sikandra, near Agra, was started by Akbar himself and completed by Jahangir (सिकंदरा में अकबर का मकबरा)

 

• It also includes the tomb of Mariam, Akbar's wife.

 

• It is regarded as unusual because Akbar began his own mausoleum.

 

• It is built in red sandstone with marble touches, differing from the all-marble Taj.

 

• The mausoleum's setting in a large garden and its tiered, pyramidal design make it unlike the dome-centred tombs of Humayun and Shah Jahan's age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb at Agra was built by Nur Jahan in white marble.

 

• Jahangir's own tomb is at Shahdara, Lahore, completed by Nur Jahan.

 

• Humayun's tomb was finished by Akbar.

 

• Akbar's other buildings include the Ibadat Khana and Tomb of Salim Chishti.

 

• Jahangir completed the tomb in 1612 with changes in the original plan, and a vast gateway with four minarets stands at its entrance.

 

NOTE

 

• Built entirely by Shah Jahan (Option 1): Shah Jahan's major works were the Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi, and the Sikandra tomb is not attributed to him.

 

• Built by Nur Jahan in white marble (Option 2): Nur Jahan built the white-marble tomb of her father Itimad-ud-Daula, using pietra dura, while the Sikandra tomb is a different structure.

 

• Constructed by Aurangzeb (Option 4): Aurangzeb built the Bibi ka Maqbara and the Moti Masjid in Delhi, with no connection to the tomb of Akbar at Sikandra.

question:
Consider the following statements about Nur Jahan:

1. Her original name was Mehrunnisa.

2. She was the widow of Sher Afghan (Ali Quli Beg).

3. She was the wife of Shah Jahan.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Nur Jahan was born Mehrunnisa, and Jahangir gave her the title Nur Jahan (Light of the World) (नूरजहाँ — मेहरुन्निसा, जहाँगीर की पत्नी)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: she was the widow of Sher Afghan (Ali Quli Beg) before she married Jahangir.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: she was the wife of Jahangir, not Shah Jahan; Shah Jahan's wife was Arjumand Bano, Mumtaz Mahal.

 

• She exercised tremendous influence over state affairs, with titles such as Badshah Begum.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Her father was Itimad-ud-Daula, the chief diwan.

 

• Her brother Asaf Khan was made Khan-i-Saman.

 

• She built her father's tomb at Agra, called the Baby Taj.

 

• Mumtaz Mahal was Asaf Khan's daughter in standard accounts.

 

• Jahangir's reign saw a faction led by Nur Jahan, Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram's circle that influenced court politics until Jahangir's death in 1627.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 2): Selecting statement 1 alone ignores that her earlier marriage to Sher Afghan is also true and often asked in exams, so the answer is incomplete.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Nur Jahan married Jahangir and not Shah Jahan, so any answer that carries the third claim is invalid; Shah Jahan's chief queen was Mumtaz Mahal.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including all three accepts the false claim that she was Shah Jahan's wife, which confuses Jahangir's queen with the empress for whom the Taj Mahal was built.

question: Jahangir's 'Zanjeer-e-Adal' (Chain of Justice) was a device installed at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Agra Fort.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jahangir installed the Zanjeer-e-Adal, a golden Chain of Justice, at Agra so that any aggrieved subject could ring the bells and seek justice (जंजीर-ए-अदल — आगरा में न्याय की जंजीर)

 

• It symbolised the emperor's accessibility to petitioners.

 

• Jahangir ruled from 1605 to 1627 and authored the Persian memoir Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.

 

• His reign is also called the golden era of painting.

 

• The chain was reported to run from the Shah Burj of the fort to a pillar on the river bank, with golden bells attached so that the emperor could hear the complaint directly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jahangir built the Shalimar garden in Srinagar, Kashmir.

 

• The Shalimar Bagh at Lahore was laid out by Shah Jahan.

 

• Jahangir's tomb is at Shahdara in Lahore.

 

• The Red Fort in Delhi was begun by Shah Jahan in 1639.

 

• Jahangir also loved nature and gardens, and he ordered the construction of the Achabal and Verinag gardens in Kashmir.

 

NOTE

 

• Fatehpur Sikri (Option 1): Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital, and the chain is not associated with that city; Jahangir's Zanjeer-e-Adal belongs to his own palace complex in Agra.

 

• Lahore Fort (Option 2): Lahore Fort is a major Mughal fort and later served as a royal residence, but the Zanjeer-e-Adal is linked specifically with Agra in the standard account.

 

• Red Fort, Delhi (Option 3): The Red Fort of Delhi was started in 1639 by Shah Jahan, years after Jahangir died, so the chain of justice cannot belong to that fort.

question: Which Sikh Guru was put to death by Jahangir after Prince Khusro's revolt?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Arjun Dev.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Khusro's revolt (Battle of Bhairowal, 1606), Jahangir had the fifth Sikh Guru Arjun Dev killed for supporting the prince (गुरु अर्जुन देव — खुसरो विद्रोह के बाद जहाँगीर द्वारा मृत्युदंड)

 

• Khusro himself was captured and blinded by his father.

 

• The incident worsened Mughal-Sikh relations and led later Gurus to take up arms.

 

• Jahangir's reign otherwise saw high cultural achievement in painting.

 

• Guru Arjun Dev had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Harmandir Sahib, so his execution made the Sikh community more conscious of its separate identity.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Guru Teg Bahadur, the ninth Guru, was killed by Aurangzeb in 1675 at Delhi.

 

• Guru Ramdas, the fourth Guru, founded Amritsar on land granted in Akbar's time.

 

• Arjun Dev compiled the Adi Granth.

 

• Hawkins reached Jahangir's court in 1608.

 

• After Arjun Dev, the sixth Guru Hargobind carried two swords of spiritual and temporal authority and was briefly jailed at Gwalior.

 

NOTE

 

• Guru Hargobind (Option 1): Guru Hargobind was Arjun Dev's son who succeeded him and survived imprisonment under Jahangir, so he was not the Guru executed after Khusro's rebellion.

 

• Guru Teg Bahadur (Option 2): Guru Teg Bahadur was executed in 1675 at Delhi on Aurangzeb's order, long after Jahangir's reign had ended, and so does not fit this episode.

 

• Guru Amardas (Option 4): Guru Amardas was the third Guru and a contemporary of Akbar, who respected him; he had died before Jahangir's accession and could not be executed by him.

question: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra, built by Nur Jahan, is notable for its use of:
option_1: Pietra dura inlay in white marble
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pietra dura inlay in white marble.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula was built wholly of white marble with floral designs of semi-precious stones, a decoration called pietra dura (इतिमाद-उद-दौला का मकबरा — पित्रा दूरा)

 

• Nur Jahan built it for her father, and it is often called the Baby Taj.

 

• The technique became far more popular under Shah Jahan and was used on a large scale at the Taj Mahal.

 

• It shows the shift from red sandstone to marble in Mughal architecture.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pietra dura inlay is called parchin kari in India.

 

• Akbar's buildings used mostly red sandstone.

 

• The Taj Mahal's marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan.

 

• Jahangir's period is also noted for the Shalimar garden in Kashmir.

 

• The Itimad-ud-Daula tomb was completed around 1628 and is a forerunner to the Taj, with inlay work set against delicate marble screens.

 

NOTE

 

• Red sandstone with no ornament (Option 2): Red sandstone without ornament is the hallmark of earlier Akbar-era structures such as Agra Fort and does not describe this elaborately inlaid white marble tomb.

 

• Glazed blue tiles (Option 3): Glazed blue tiles are associated with Persian and Lahore Fort decoration, while Itimad-ud-Daula is known for stone inlay and marble rather than ceramic tile.

 

• Brick and lime plaster (Option 4): Brick and lime plaster would not match a monument described as wholly of white marble with inlaid floral designs made of semi-precious stones.

question:
Match the works with their authors.

Column A: (a) Akbar Nama (b) Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (c) Shahjahan Nama (d) Humayunama

Column B: (i) Inayat Khan (ii) Gulbadan Begum (iii) Abul Fazal (iv) Jahangir
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Akbar Nama was written by Abul Fazal, so (a)-(iii) (अकबरनामा — अबुल फजल)

 

• The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri is the autobiography of Jahangir, written in Persian, so (b)-(iv).

 

• The Shahjahan Nama was written by Inayat Khan, so (c)-(i).

 

• The Humayunama was written by Gulbadan Begum, so (d)-(ii).

 

• Together these books are the main chronicles of the first Mughal century and a half: memoirs by Babur and Jahangir, a biography of Humayun and official histories of Akbar and Shah Jahan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Babur authored the Tuzuk-i-Baburi in Turkish.

 

• The Alamgir Nama relates to Aurangzeb.

 

• Aurangzeb compiled the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri.

 

• Abul Fazal also authored the Ain-i-Akbari.

 

• Mughal rulers took a particular interest in memoir writing, and Jahangir's Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri also records events of his reign and his views on art and nature.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This exchanges Akbar Nama and Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, giving Abul Fazal the emperor's own memoir; the Tuzuk is Jahangir's autobiography while Abul Fazal authored Akbar's chronicle.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 3): This pairs the Tuzuk with Inayat Khan and Shahjahan Nama with Jahangir, so the author of Shah Jahan's biography is wrongly connected with the memoir of Jahangir.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This gives Shahjahan Nama to Gulbadan Begum and Humayunama to Inayat Khan, so the writers of two different court biographies are interchanged.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Taj Mahal:

1. It was built between 1631 and 1653.

2. Its chief architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

3. It was built in memory of Nur Jahan.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Taj Mahal was constructed from 1631 to 1653 at Agra (ताजमहल — 1631 से 1653 तक निर्मित)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the chief architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahori and the chief constructor was Ustad Isa.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: it was built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Bano).

 

• It uses white marble from Makrana in Rajasthan and the pietra dura art form.

 

• The monument stands on the bank of the Yamuna at Agra and combines Persian, Turkish and Indian elements, so it is seen as the summit of Mughal architectural development.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Taj Mahal was inspired by Humayun's Tomb.

 

• The Quranic inscriptions were written by Amanat Khan Siraji.

 

• Mumtaz Mahal bore 14 children, of whom 7 survived.

 

• Shah Jahan's reign is the golden era of Mughal architecture.

 

• After Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 in Burhanpur during childbirth, her body was brought to Agra and placed in the finished monument.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Choosing statement 1 alone leaves out the architect, Ustad Ahmad Lahori, which is a true detail of the monument's construction.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Nur Jahan was Jahangir's queen, so the third claim about the dedication fails and drags the pair down; the Taj Mahal commemorates Mumtaz Mahal, wife of Shah Jahan.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three would accept the incorrect dedication to Nur Jahan, though the Taj Mahal is the memorial of Shah Jahan's wife Arjumand Bano Begum.

question: The Red Fort at Delhi, begun in 1639, was designed by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Red Fort at Delhi, with the Rang Mahal, Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas, was built by Shah Jahan under architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori (लाल किला — शाहजहाँ, वास्तुकार उस्ताद अहमद लाहौरी)

 

• Construction began in 1639 and was completed after about nine years.

 

• Ahmad Lahori was also the chief architect of the Taj Mahal.

 

• Fort-building reached its climax in Shah Jahan's reign.

 

• The fort's walls of red sandstone gave it its name, and its halls were the setting for the Peacock Throne ceremonies and the daily public audiences of the emperor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shah Jahan shifted the capital to Shahjahanabad in 1648.

 

• The Moti Masjid inside the Agra Fort is by Shah Jahan.

 

• The Peacock Throne was commissioned by him.

 

• Delhi's Jama Masjid is of red sandstone.

 

• The Red Fort became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, and the Indian prime minister addresses the nation from its ramparts on Independence Day.

 

NOTE

 

• Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (Option 1): Mirak Mirza Ghiyas designed Humayun's Tomb in Delhi in the sixteenth century, which is a different monument from the Red Fort of Shah Jahan.

 

• Mir Baqi (Option 3): Mir Baqi was Babur's commander who built the mosque at Ayodhya in 1527-28, and nothing links him with seventeenth-century Shah Jahan's fort.

 

• Amanat Khan Siraji (Option 4): Amanat Khan Siraji authored the Quranic calligraphy on the Taj Mahal, which makes him a calligrapher and not the architect of the Red Fort.

question: Shah Jahan shifted his capital in 1648 to Shahjahanabad, which is the present:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Old Delhi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1648 the capital was moved to Shahjahanabad, present Old Delhi, counted as the seventh city of Delhi (शाहजहाँनाबाद — वर्तमान पुरानी दिल्ली, दिल्ली का सातवाँ नगर)

 

• The Red Fort stood at the heart of the new city.

 

• Earlier, Agra had been the Mughal capital from Babur's time.

 

• Shah Jahan reigned 1627-1658 and was deposed by Aurangzeb after the war of succession.

 

• The shift to the new city was a statement of imperial confidence, and the planned town with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid became the centre of Mughal power until 1857.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar had shifted from Fatehpur Sikri to Lahore.

 

• Shah Jahan declared Dara Shikoh his heir in 1657.

 

• Dara, Shuja, Aurangzeb and Murad Bakhsh were the four sons.

 

• Aurangzeb defeated Dara in the struggle.

 

• The new capital was built on the right bank of the Yamuna, with Chandni Chowk laid out as the central market street.

 

NOTE

 

• Fatehpur Sikri (Option 1): Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned by Akbar because of water shortage and administrative reasons, long before Shah Jahan; it never served him as capital.

 

• Lahore (Option 2): Lahore was used by Akbar as capital in the later phase of his reign and was not the city founded by Shah Jahan in 1648.

 

• Agra (Option 3): Agra was the Mughal capital before 1648 and Shah Jahan moved away from it, so Shahjahanabad cannot be the same as Agra.

question: Aurangzeb reimposed jiziya on non-Muslims in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1679.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurangzeb reimposed jiziya in 1679, which Akbar had abolished in 1564 (जज़िया का पुनः आरोपण, 1679 — औरंगजेब)

 

• In 1659 he had earlier reimposed the pilgrimage tax.

 

• He adopted anti-Hindu measures such as banning some festivals and destroying temples including the Kashi Vishwanath and Keshav Rai temples.

 

• Under him the empire reached its greatest extent.

 

• The reimposition marked a break from the inclusive policy begun by Akbar and was followed by opposition from Rajputs and Marathas, who saw it as an attack on non-Muslim subjects.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aurangzeb was born in 1618 and reigned from 1658 to 1707.

 

• His title Alamgir means world conqueror.

 

• He earned a living by selling copies of the Quran.

 

• He compiled the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri.

 

• The jiziya was a tax on non-Muslims in exchange for patronage and exemption from military service, levied under several Delhi Sultanate rulers and then abolished by Akbar before being revived by Aurangzeb.

 

NOTE

 

• 1659 (Option 1): 1659 is the year of the pilgrimage tax being imposed again, a separate measure from the jiziya which came two decades later.

 

• 1675 (Option 2): 1675 is the year of the execution of the ninth Sikh Guru Teg Bahadur at Delhi, not the date of reimposing jiziya.

 

• 1681 (Option 4): 1681 is the year of the revolt of Prince Akbar, Aurangzeb's son, supported by Sambhaji, and it does not mark the jiziya.

question: Guru Teg Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was executed at Delhi in 1675 on the orders of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aurangzeb.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1675 the ninth Sikh Guru, Guru Teg Bahadur, was executed at Delhi by Aurangzeb (गुरु तेग बहादुर की शहादत, 1675 — औरंगजेब)

 

• It was part of Aurangzeb's anti-Hindu and religiously rigid policy.

 

• Earlier, Jahangir had executed the fifth Guru Arjun Dev.

 

• The event led his son Guru Gobind Singh to organise the Sikhs militarily.

 

• The death of the Guru in Delhi is remembered with the Gurdwara Sis Ganj at the spot in Chandni Chowk, and the event turned the Sikhs toward militarisation under Guru Gobind Singh.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar and was buried at Daulatabad.

 

• Jizya was reimposed four years later in 1679.

 

• Bahadur Shah I ruled 1707-12.

 

• He took the title Alamgir.

 

• Teg Bahadur is known in Sikh tradition as Hind di Chadar, or the Shield of India, for giving his life in defence of religious freedom.

 

NOTE

 

• Jahangir (Option 2): Jahangir had the fifth Guru, Arjun Dev, executed in 1606 after Khusro's revolt, and so the execution of the ninth Guru was not his act.

 

• Shah Jahan (Option 3): Shah Jahan reigned from 1627 to 1658 and had been deposed by 1658, so he could not give the order in 1675.

 

• Bahadur Shah I (Option 4): Bahadur Shah I ruled from 1707 to 1712, more than thirty years after the Guru's execution in 1675, so the order cannot be his.

question: Aurangzeb was known as 'Zinda Pir' (Living Saint) because he:
option_2: Gave away the treasury to the poor
option_3: Lived a saintly life and earned his own money by selling copies of the Quran
option_4: Was a disciple of Sheikh Salim Chishti
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lived a saintly life and earned his own money by selling copies of the Quran.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurangzeb was called Zinda Pir because he lived like a saint and never took a penny from the treasury; he earned by selling written copies of the Quran (जिंदा पीर — औरंगजेब का संयमी जीवन)

 

• He did not consume wine and led a simple, disciplined life.

 

• He was one of the ablest Mughal kings, with the title Alamgir.

 

• He ruled from 1658 to 1707 and spent the last decades in the Deccan.

 

• The title reflected the contrast between his austere personal habits and the vast power he held, which made him a respected and feared figure among the orthodox.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar followed Sheikh Salim Chishti.

 

• Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in 1707.

 

• His biography, the Alamgir Nama, was by Kazim Shirazi.

 

• His wife Dilras Bano Begum is also known as Rabia Biwi.

 

• Aurangzeb also banned music at court, abolished the jharokha darshan and discouraged the Navroz celebrations.

 

• Aurangzeb also barred music at court and discouraged lavish festivals, which differs from the cultural patronage of Akbar and Shah Jahan.

 

NOTE

 

• Founded a new religion (Option 1): Founding a new religion is associated with Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi, and Aurangzeb followed orthodox Islam rather than starting any new faith.

 

• Gave away the treasury to the poor (Option 2): Giving away the state treasury is not the reason for the title; the point is that he refused to draw personal income from it, not that he distributed it.

 

• Was a disciple of Sheikh Salim Chishti (Option 4): Sheikh Salim Chishti was the Sufi saint followed by Akbar, who named his son Salim after him, and the title Zinda Pir has no relation to this devotion.

question: The Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad, called the 'Taj of the Deccan', was built in memory of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rabia-ud-Daurani.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bibi ka Maqbara, the 'Taj of the Deccan', was built for Aurangzeb's wife Rabia-ud-Daurani (Dilras Bano Begum) (बीबी का मकबरा — औरंगाबाद, रबिया-उद-दौरानी)

 

• It is often called the second Taj Mahal because it imitates the design of the Taj.

 

• Aurangzeb also built the Moti Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque at Lahore.

 

• Mosque and monument building were less lavish than under Shah Jahan.

 

• Though the mausoleum is smaller and plainer than the original, it is the most prominent Mughal monument in the Deccan and shows the architectural taste of Aurangzeb's reign.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aurangzeb was born in 1618.

 

• Under him the empire was the largest single state in India.

 

• He died at Ahmednagar and was buried at Daulatabad.

 

• He reimposed jiziya in 1679.

 

• Rabia-ud-Daurani died in 1657 and her tomb was built by her son Azam Shah under Aurangzeb's direction, with Ata-ullah as chief architect.

 

NOTE

 

• Mumtaz Mahal (Option 1): Mumtaz Mahal is commemorated by the original Taj Mahal at Agra and not by the Aurangabad tomb, so naming her mixes up the model with the imitation.

 

• Nur Jahan (Option 3): Nur Jahan's resting place lies at Shahdara in Lahore near Jahangir, and she is not the subject of the Bibi ka Maqbara in the Deccan.

 

• Hamida Banu Begum (Option 4): Hamida Banu Begum was Humayun's wife and Akbar's mother, associated with Humayun's Tomb and not with a monument at Aurangabad.

question: Which later Mughal ruler, who came to the throne at the age of 63, was known as 'Buddha Badshah'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bahadur Shah I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bahadur Shah I (1707-12) took the throne at age 63, the oldest Mughal ruler of Delhi, hence called Buddha Badshah; he took the title Shah Alam I (बहादुर शाह प्रथम — बूढ़ा बादशाह)

 

• He was the son of Aurangzeb and won the war of succession after his father's death.

 

• His successor Jahandar Shah (1712-13) was his son.

 

• Farrukh Siyar (1713-19) was a grandson of Bahadur Shah I and was assassinated by nobles.

 

• At 63 he was the oldest man to take the Mughal throne, and his reign was short and marked by the weakening of central authority soon after his father's long rule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Muhammad Shah (1719-48) was called Rangeela Badshah.

 

• Ahmad Shah made Safdarjung wazir.

 

• Alamgir II was ruling when Plassey was fought in 1757.

 

• Bahadur Shah II was the last Mughal.

 

• Jahandar Shah, son of Bahadur Shah I, came to power with the help of the nobleman Zulfiqar Khan after a war of succession among the sons.

 

NOTE

 

• Jahandar Shah (Option 1): Jahandar Shah ruled only for about a year (1712-13) and is not remembered for his age, so the title Buddha Badshah does not belong to him.

 

• Farrukh Siyar (Option 2): Farrukh Siyar was a young grandson of Bahadur Shah I who was later assassinated, and he is not the aged ruler of the title.

 

• Muhammad Shah (Option 4): Muhammad Shah, nicknamed Rangeela, ruled 1719-48 and is remembered for pleasure-loving ways, not for being an old king at accession.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Farrukh Siyar was assassinated by his nobles.

2. Alamgir II was assassinated by his nobles.

3. Bahadur Shah II was assassinated by his nobles.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Farrukh Siyar (1713-19), grandson of Bahadur Shah I, was assassinated by his nobles (फर्रुखसियर और आलमगीर द्वितीय — सरदारों द्वारा हत्या)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Alamgir II (1754-59), during whose reign the Battle of Plassey (1757) took place, was also assassinated by his nobles.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) was exiled by the British to Rangoon after the 1857 revolt and died there in 1862.

 

• So only the first two are correct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bahadur Shah II's wazir in 1857 was Bakht Khan.

 

• His sons were killed by the British.

 

• Plassey lasted only a short time.

 

• Shah Alam II (1759-1806) reigned for nearly fifty years.

 

• The Sayyid brothers, Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali Khan, were the kingmakers who influenced the downfall of Farrukh Siyar in 1719.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Alamgir II (1754-59), in whose reign the Battle of Plassey was fought, was also killed by his nobles, so leaving out the second claim gives an incomplete answer.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Bahadur Shah II met a different end, being exiled by the British to Rangoon, so tying him to assassination by nobles is wrong and the pair cannot be accepted.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Taking all three mistakes the fate of Bahadur Shah II; he died in 1862 at Rangoon in captivity, far from his Delhi court.

question: Bahadur Shah II 'Zafar', the last Mughal emperor, was exiled after the 1857 revolt to:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rangoon.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After leading the 1857 revolt at Delhi, Bahadur Shah II was exiled by the British to Rangoon in Burma (Myanmar), where he died in 1862 (बहादुर शाह ज़फ़र — रंगून निर्वासन)

 

• He was the son of Akbar II and ruled from 1837 to 1858.

 

• His wazir in 1857 was Bakht Khan.

 

• The British killed his heirs, ending the dynasty.

 

• The fall of the dynasty followed the suppression of the revolt, as the British ended even the nominal Mughal rule and took over direct control in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar II gave the title Raja to Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

 

• Shah Alam II was the first Mughal appointed by the British.

 

• Delhi fell to the British in September 1857.

 

• He was also a Persian and Urdu poet under the pen name Zafar.

 

• Bakht Khan, a cavalry officer, led the sepoys who gathered in Delhi in 1857, and Bahadur Shah was recognised as the symbolic head of the revolt.

 

NOTE

 

• Andaman (Option 2): The Andaman Islands were used by the British as a penal colony for revolutionaries after 1857, but Bahadur Shah II himself was not sent there.

 

• Calcutta (Option 3): Calcutta was the British capital of India then, and he was not detained in that city for the rest of his life.

 

• Mandalay (Option 4): Mandalay was the capital of the Burmese kings, and the Mughal emperor was kept at Rangoon, not Mandalay, until he died.

question: Akbar II (1806-37) conferred the title of 'Raja' on which reformer and sent him to London as his envoy?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Akbar II gave the title Raja to Ram Mohan Roy and sent him to London as his ambassador (अकबर द्वितीय — राजा राममोहन राय को राजा की उपाधि)

 

• Ram Mohan Roy is called the Father of the Bengal Renaissance.

 

• Akbar II was the father of Bahadur Shah II.

 

• By his time Mughal power was restricted to the Red Fort in Delhi.

 

• His reign shows how limited Mughal authority had become by the early nineteenth century, as the emperor lived on a pension from the East India Company while retaining ceremonial titles.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj.

 

• Shah Alam II was the first Mughal to be appointed by the British.

 

• Ahmad Shah made Safdarjung the wazir.

 

• Muhammad Shah had the title Rangeela.

 

• The Mughal emperors after 1803 lived under the patronage of the East India Company in the Red Fort, and the Company stopped issuing coins in the Mughal name by 1835.

 

NOTE

 

• Dayananda Saraswati (Option 1): Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, long after Akbar II died in 1837, and he was not sent to England by a Mughal.

 

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (Option 3): Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar worked for widow remarriage in mid-nineteenth century Bengal, after Akbar II's death, so the title cannot have been conferred on him.

 

• Keshab Chandra Sen (Option 4): Keshab Chandra Sen was a Brahmo leader who visited England in 1870, decades after the Mughal ruler Akbar II died.

question: The Panch Mahal in Fatehpur Sikri is built on the pattern of a:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Buddhist vihara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The architectural pattern of the five-storeyed Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri is based on a Buddhist vihara (पंच महल — बौद्ध विहार पर आधारित)

 

• It is also called the 'Dream in Stone', while the Taj Mahal is the 'Dream in Marble'.

 

• Fatehpur Sikri, 36 km from Agra, was Akbar's palace-cum-fort complex, the City of Victory.

 

• Many buildings there show Gujarati and other regional styles, apart from Jodha Bai's palace.

 

• The Panch Mahal had open pillared storeys, each smaller than the one below, so it served as a breezy pavilion from which court ladies could enjoy the view of the courtyard.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Jama Masjid and the Buland Darwaza are the major religious structures there.

 

• Agra Fort, Lahore Fort and Allahabad Fort were also built by Akbar.

 

• Mughal architecture blended Persian, Islamic, Turkish and Indian styles.

 

• Akbar made Persian the official language.

 

• The Diwan-i-Am at Fatehpur Sikri was used for public hearings and the Diwan-i-Khas for private discussions, and the Anup Talao tank lies near the Diwan-i-Khas.

 

NOTE

 

• Jain temple (Option 2): A Jain temple is not the model named for the Panch Mahal; this palace takes its stepped storeys from a Buddhist vihara and not a Jain shrine.

 

• Rajput fortress (Option 3): A Rajput fortress is not the pattern for the Panch Mahal, although Rajput influence appears in some Fatehpur Sikri palaces built for Akbar's Rajput wives.

 

• Persian mosque (Option 4): A Persian mosque would suggest domes and iwans, whereas the Panch Mahal is a five-tier pavilion with open columns, so that pattern fits poorly.

question: Captain William Hawkins, who came to Jahangir's court in 1608 as an envoy of the East India Company, was given the title:
solution_text:
The correct answer is English Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Captain William Hawkins reached Jahangir's court in 1608 as a representative of the East India Company, and the emperor gave him the title English Khan (विलियम हॉकिन्स — जहाँगीर द्वारा 'इंग्लिश खान' की उपाधि)

 

• He sought trading permission for the English at Surat.

 

• In 1615 Sir Thomas Roe, an ambassador of King James I, visited Jahangir.

 

• Ralph Fitch had been the first Englishman at Akbar's court in 1585.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pietro della Valle, an Italian traveller, visited during Jahangir's reign.

 

• Tobacco, brought by the Portuguese, began to be produced in his time.

 

• The poet Surdas authored the Sur Sagar in this period.

 

• Jahangir ruled from 1605 to 1627.

 

• The Portuguese had brought tobacco into India, and the Mughals took up its cultivation and use in the early seventeenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Khan-i-Khana (Option 1): Khan-i-Khana was the title of Bairam Khan and later his son Abdul Rahim, both Mughal nobles, and was never conferred on the English envoy.

 

• Mirza Raja (Option 3): Mirza Raja was a Mughal honour associated with Rajput nobles like Jai Singh of Amber, and it was not given to the English agent.

 

• Raja Bahadur (Option 4): Raja Bahadur is a later general honorific, and the Mughal ruler did not give Hawkins this title; the record names him with the playful English Khan.

question: Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar. His tomb is located at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Daulatabad (Khuldabad).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar in Maharashtra and was buried at Daulatabad, near Aurangabad (औरंगजेब की मृत्यु 1707, अहमदनगर; दफन दौलताबाद)

 

• He spent the last decades of his life in the Deccan campaigns against Bijapur, Golconda and the Marathas.

 

• Under him the empire reached its greatest extent, becoming the largest single state in India.

 

• He compiled the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri, a collection of Islamic law.

 

• The grave in the Deccan is plain and open to the sky, in keeping with his personal wish for simplicity and his austere reputation among contemporaries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• His biography is the Alamgir Nama.

 

• Bahadur Shah I succeeded him in 1707.

 

• His wife Dilras Bano Begum's tomb is at Aurangabad.

 

• He built the Moti Masjid in Delhi.

 

• Aurangzeb's long Deccan war drained the treasury and forced the Mughal state to maintain a large army in the south for more than twenty years.

 

NOTE

 

• Agra (Option 2): Agra holds the Taj Mahal and tombs of Shah Jahan and Akbar's relatives, but Aurangzeb chose an unpretentious grave in the Deccan and was not buried there.

 

• Delhi (Option 3): Delhi has Humayun's tomb and the Red Fort, but Aurangzeb died far away in the south and was laid to rest in the Deccan instead.

 

• Lahore (Option 4): Lahore is the resting place of Jahangir at Shahdara and Nur Jahan, not of Aurangzeb who died in Maharashtra and was buried in the Deccan.
